go:1638.title: GATE CSE 1998 | Question: 1.1
go:1638.question:
A die is rolled three times. The probability that exactly one odd number turns up among the three outcomes is

  1. $\dfrac{1}{6}$  
  2. $\dfrac{3}{8}$  
  3. $\dfrac{1}{8}$  
  4. $\dfrac{1}{2}$

detailed_solution.concept: Engineering Mathematics - Probability
detailed_solution.markdown:
Each die roll is odd with probability $1/2$. Choose which of the three rolls is the sole odd result in $\binom31$ ways; each such parity pattern has probability $(1/2)^3$. Therefore,

$$P=\binom31\left(\frac12\right)^3=\frac38.$$

**Option B.**

go:1639.title: GATE CSE 1998 | Question: 1.2
go:1639.question:
Consider the following set of equations

  • $x+2y=5$
  • $4x+8y=12$
  • $3x+6y+3z=15$

This set

  1. has unique solution
  2. has no solution
  3. has finite number of solutions
  4. has infinite number of solutions

detailed_solution.concept: Engineering Mathematics - Linear Algebra
detailed_solution.markdown:
The second equation has a left side exactly twice that of the first: $4x+8y=2(x+2y)$. If the first equation $x+2y=5$ held, doubling it would give $4x+8y=10$, contradicting the second equation's requirement $4x+8y=12$. No pair $(x,y)$ can satisfy both equations, so the full system has no solution.

**Option B.**

go:1640.title: GATE CSE 1998 | Question: 1.3
go:1640.question:
Which of the following statements applies to the bisection method used for finding roots of functions:

  1. converges within a few iterations

  2. guaranteed to work for all continuous functions

  3. is faster than the Newton-Raphson method

  4. requires that there be no error in determining the sign of the function

detailed_solution.concept: Engineering Mathematics - Numerical Methods and the Bisection Method
detailed_solution.markdown:
### 1. Conceptual Framework & Theoretical Foundation
The **Bisection Method** is a bracketing numerical method for finding real roots of a continuous function $f(x) = 0$.
It is grounded in the **Intermediate Value Theorem (Bolzano's Theorem)**:
> If a real-valued function $f(x)$ is continuous on the closed interval $[a, b]$, and $f(a) \cdot f(b) < 0$ (the function values at the endpoints have opposite signs), then there exists at least one value $c \in (a, b)$ such that $f(c) = 0$.

### 2. Analysis of the Statements
- **Statement A: "converges within a few iterations"**
  - **Incorrect.** The bisection method converges linearly with a convergence rate of $1/2$ per iteration ($e_{n+1} = 0.5 e_n$). Reducing error by a factor of $10^{-6}$ requires approximately $20$ iterations, which is relatively slow compared to higher-order methods.

- **Statement B: "guaranteed to work for all continuous functions"**
  - **Correct.** Provided the initial interval $[a, b]$ brackets a root ($f(a) \cdot f(b) < 0$) and $f(x)$ is continuous on $[a, b]$, the bisection method is mathematically **guaranteed to converge** to a root.

- **Statement C: "is faster than the Newton-Raphson method"**
  - **Incorrect.** Newton-Raphson exhibits **quadratic convergence** ($e_{n+1} \approx C e_n^2$, doubling the number of correct decimal digits each iteration), whereas bisection exhibits only linear convergence.

- **Statement D: "requires that there be no error in determining the sign of the function"**
  - **Incorrect.** While sign determination is used to select sub-intervals, small floating-point errors away from the root do not invalidate the algorithm; the defining theoretical property is guaranteed convergence under continuity.

**Correct Answer: Option B**

go:1641.title: GATE CSE 1998 | Question: 1.4
go:1641.question:
Consider the function $y=|x|$ in the interval $[-1, 1]$. In this interval, the function is

  1. continuous and differentiable
  2. continuous but not differentiable
  3. differentiable but not continuous
  4. neither continuous nor differentiable

detailed_solution.concept: Engineering Mathematics - Calculus
detailed_solution.markdown:
The absolute-value function is continuous everywhere, including at $x=0$. For $x>0$ its derivative is $1$, and for $x<0$ its derivative is $-1$. Since the one-sided derivatives at $0$ differ, the function is not differentiable there; hence it is not differentiable on the whole interval.

**Option B.**

go:1642.title: GATE CSE 1998 | Question: 1.5
go:1642.question:
What is the converse of the following assertion?

  • I stay only if you go
  1. I stay if you go
  2. If I stay then you go
  3. If you do not go then I do not stay
  4. If I do not stay then you go

detailed_solution.concept: Discrete Mathematics - Propositional Logic
detailed_solution.markdown:
“I stay only if you go” means that my staying implies your going: $S\to G$. The converse swaps the hypothesis and conclusion, giving $G\to S$: if you go, I stay.

**Option A.**

go:1643.title: GATE CSE 1998 | Question: 1.6
go:1643.question:
Suppose $A$ is a finite set with $n$ elements. The number of elements in the largest equivalence relation of A is

  1. $n$
  2. $n^2$
  3. $1$
  4. $n+1$

detailed_solution.concept: Discrete Mathematics - Relations
detailed_solution.markdown:
An equivalence relation on $A$ can contain at most all ordered pairs in $A\times A$. The universal relation $A\times A$ is itself reflexive, symmetric, and transitive, so it is the largest equivalence relation. Since $|A|=n$, it contains $n^2$ ordered pairs.

**Option B ($n^2$).**

go:1644.title: GATE CSE 1998 | Question: 1.7
go:1644.question:
Let $R_1$ and $R_2$ be two equivalence relations on a set. Consider the following assertions:

  1. $R_1 \cup R_2$ is an equivalence relation
  2. $R_1 \cap R_2$ is an equivalence relation

Which of the following is correct?

  1. Both assertions are true
  2. Assertions (i) is true but assertions (ii) is not true
  3. Assertions (ii) is true but assertions (i) is not true
  4. Neither (i) nor (ii) is true

detailed_solution.concept: Discrete Mathematics - Relations
detailed_solution.markdown:
The intersection is always an equivalence relation: each relation contains every diagonal pair, and symmetry and transitivity are preserved when a pair must belong to both relations.

The union need not be transitive. On $\{1,2,3\}$, let one equivalence partition be $\{1,2\},\{3\}$ and the other be $\{1\},\{2,3\}$. Their union contains $(1,2)$ and $(2,3)$ but not $(1,3)$. Thus (ii) is true while (i) is not.

**Option C.**

go:1645.title: GATE CSE 1998 | Question: 1.8
go:1645.question:
The number of functions from an $m$ element set to an $n$ element set is

  1. $m + n$
  2. $m^n$
  3. $n^m$
  4. $m*n$

detailed_solution.concept: Discrete Mathematics - Combinatory
detailed_solution.markdown:
For each of the $m$ domain elements, a function independently chooses one of the $n$ codomain elements as its image. Multiplying the $n$ choices for each of $m$ inputs gives $n^m$ functions.

**Option C ($n^m$).**

go:1646.title: GATE CSE 1998 | Question: 1.9
go:1646.question:
If the regular set $A$ is represented by $A = (01 + 1)^*$ and the regular set $B$ is represented by $B = \left(\left(01\right)^*1^*\right)^*$, which of the following is true?

  1. $A \subset B$
  2. $B \subset A$
  3. $A$ and $B$ are incomparable
  4. $A = B$

detailed_solution.concept: Theory of Computation - Regular Expression Equivalence and Algebraic Identities
detailed_solution.markdown:
### 1. Problem Formulation & Scope
We are given two regular expressions defining languages over the alphabet $\Sigma = \{0, 1\}$:
- $A = (01 + 1)^*$
- $B = \left((01)^* 1^*\right)^*$

We must determine the relationship between $A$ and $B$ (whether $A \subset B$, $B \subset A$, incomparable, or $A = B$).

### 2. Algebraic Regular Expression Identities
Recall the fundamental Kleene star expansion theorem for any regular expressions $R$ and $S$:
$$\left(R^* S^*\right)^* = (R + S)^*$$

*Proof of Identity:*
- **Part 1 ($(R+S)^* \subseteq (R^* S^*)^*$):** Any string in $(R + S)^*$ is a finite sequence of blocks where each block is either an $R$ or an $S$. In $(R^* S^*)^*$, each factor can generate arbitrary sequences of $R$'s followed by arbitrary sequences of $S$'s. Since a single $R$ can be written as $R^1 S^0$ and a single $S$ can be written as $R^0 S^1$, any sequence of $R$'s and $S$'s can be formed by $(R^* S^*)^*$.
- **Part 2 ($(R^* S^*)^* \subseteq (R+S)^*)$:** Every string generated by $(R^* S^*)^*$ consists of concatenated strings from $R$ and $S$. Since $(R+S)^*$ generates all possible concatenations of strings from $R$ and $S$, every string in $(R^* S^*)^*$ is in $(R+S)^*$.
- Therefore, $(R^* S^*)^* = (R + S)^*$.

### 3. Application to Given Sets
Let:
$$R = 01 \quad \text{and} \quad S = 1$$
Substituting into the identity:
$$B = \left((01)^* 1^*\right)^* = (01 + 1)^* = A$$

Therefore:
$$A = B$$

### 4. Language Characterization
Both $A$ and $B$ generate the exact language of all strings over $\{0, 1\}$ such that every `0` is immediately followed by a `1` (i.e., strings containing no substring `00` and not ending in `0`).

**Correct Answer: Option D ($A = B$)**

go:1647.title: GATE CSE 1998 | Question: 1.10
go:1647.question:
Which of the following set can be recognized by a Deterministic Finite state Automaton?

  1. The numbers $1, 2, 4, 8, \dots 2^n, \dots$ written in binary

  2. The numbers $1, 2, 4, 8,\dots 2^n, \dots$  written in unary

  3. The set of binary string in which the number of zeros is the same as the number of ones.

  4. The set $\{1, 101, 11011, 1110111, \dots\}$

detailed_solution.concept: Theory of Computation - Languages Recognizable by Deterministic Finite Automata (DFA)
detailed_solution.markdown:
### 1. Conceptual Framework & Regularity Criterion
A language $L$ can be recognized by a **Deterministic Finite state Automaton (DFA)** if and only if $L$ is a **Regular Language**.
A language requiring unbounded memory to count or match symbols is non-regular by the Pumping Lemma.

### 2. Analysis of the Candidate Sets
1. **Set A: The numbers $1, 2, 4, 8, \dots, 2^n, \dots$ written in binary**
   - The powers of $2$ written in standard binary notation are:
     $$2^0 = 1_2, \quad 2^1 = 10_2, \quad 2^2 = 100_2, \quad 2^3 = 1000_2, \quad \dots, \quad 2^n = 100\dots 0_2$$
   - This set of strings corresponds precisely to the regular expression:
     $$L = 10^*$$
   - A DFA with $2$ states easily recognizes $10^*$:
     - State $q_0$ (start): on input `1`, transition to accepting state $q_1$; on input `0`, transition to dead state $q_d$.
     - State $q_1$ (accepting): on input `0`, self-loop to $q_1$; on input `1`, transition to $q_d$.
   - Because $10^*$ is regular, it is **recognizable by a DFA**.

2. **Set B: The numbers $1, 2, 4, 8, \dots, 2^n, \dots$ written in unary**
   - In unary, $L = \{1^{2^n} \mid n \ge 0\}$.
   - The gap between successive string lengths is $2^{n+1} - 2^n = 2^n$, which grows unboundedly. By the Pumping Lemma, $L$ is **not regular**.

3. **Set C: Binary strings with an equal number of zeros and ones**
   - $L = \{w \in \{0, 1\}^* \mid N_0(w) = N_1(w)\}$.
   - Requires an unbounded counter to track the difference $N_0(w) - N_1(w)$. It is a deterministic context-free language (DCFL), **not regular**.

4. **Set D: The set $\{1, 101, 11011, 1110111, \dots\}$**
   - Corresponds to $L = \{1^n 0 1^n \mid n \ge 0\}$.
   - Requires matching the count of `1`s before and after `0`. By the Pumping Lemma, $L$ is **not regular**.

**Correct Answer: Option A**

go:1648.title: GATE CSE 1998 | Question: 1.11
go:1648.question:
Regarding the power of recognition of languages, which of the following statements is false?

  1. The non-deterministic finite-state automata are equivalent to deterministic finite-state automata.

  2. Non-deterministic Push-down automata are equivalent to deterministic Push-down automata.

  3. Non-deterministic Turing machines are equivalent to deterministic Turing machines.

  4. Multi-tape Turing machines are available are equivalent to Single-tape Turing machines.

detailed_solution.concept: Theory of Computation - Computational Power of Deterministic vs Non-Deterministic Automata
detailed_solution.markdown:
### 1. Conceptual Framework & Automata Equivalence
In formal language theory, adding non-determinism increases computational recognition power for some machine models, but not for others.

### 2. Evaluation of Statements
- **Statement A: "The non-deterministic finite-state automata are equivalent to deterministic finite-state automata."**
  - **True.** By the Subset Construction (Rabin-Scott theorem), every $N$-state NFA can be converted into an equivalent DFA with at most $2^N$ states. Both recognize precisely the class of **Regular Languages**.

- **Statement B: "Non-deterministic Push-down automata are equivalent to deterministic Push-down automata."**
  - **FALSE.** A Non-deterministic Pushdown Automaton (NPDA) recognizes the entire class of **Context-Free Languages (CFLs)**. A Deterministic Pushdown Automaton (DPDA) recognizes strictly the subclass of **Deterministic Context-Free Languages (DCFLs)**.
  - Because $\text{DCFL} \subsetneq \text{CFL}$, DPDAs are strictly less powerful than NPDAs.
  - *Counterexample:* The language of even-length palindromes $L = \{w w^R \mid w \in \{0, 1\}^*\}$ is a CFL recognizable by an NPDA (guessing the midpoint), but cannot be recognized by any DPDA.

- **Statement C: "Non-deterministic Turing machines are equivalent to deterministic Turing machines."**
  - **True.** A Deterministic Turing Machine (DTM) can simulate a Non-deterministic Turing Machine (NDTM) by performing a breadth-first search of the non-deterministic computation tree. Both recognize the exact class of **Turing-recognizable (Recursively Enumerable) languages**.

- **Statement D: "Multi-tape Turing machines are equivalent to Single-tape Turing machines."**
  - **True.** A standard single-tape Turing machine can simulate any $k$-tape Turing machine by interleaving the contents of the $k$ tapes with track markers, with a quadratic time overhead ($T(n) \to O(T(n)^2)$).

### 3. Conclusion
The statement that is false is **Option B**.

**Correct Answer: Option B**

go:1649.title: GATE CSE 1998 | Question: 1.12
go:1649.question:
The string $1101$ does not belong to the set represented by

  1. $110^*(0 + 1)$
  2. $1(0 + 1)^*101$
  3. $(10)^*(01)^*(00 + 11)^*$
  4. $(00 + (11)^*0)^*$

detailed_solution.concept: Theory of Computation - String Membership in Regular Expressions
detailed_solution.markdown:
### 1. Problem Formulation & Scope
We are given the target string:
$$w = 1101$$
We need to determine which regular expression(s) **cannot** generate $w$ (i.e., $w$ does not belong to the set).

### 2. Testing String Membership for Each Regular Expression
1. **Expression A: $110^*(0 + 1)$**
   - Decomposing $w = 1101$:
     - Prefix: `11` (matches $11$)
     - Middle: `0` (matches $0^*$ for exponent $1$)
     - Suffix: `1` (matches $(0 + 1)$)
   - Since $11 \cdot 0^1 \cdot 1 = 1101$, $1101$ **belongs** to set A.

2. **Expression B: $1(0 + 1)^* 101$**
   - Decomposing $w = 1101$:
     - Prefix: `1` (matches leading $1$)
     - Middle: $\varepsilon$ (matches $(0 + 1)^*$ with zero iterations)
     - Suffix: `101` (matches trailing $101$)
   - Since $1 \cdot \varepsilon \cdot 101 = 1101$, $1101$ **belongs** to set B.

3. **Expression C: $(10)^* (01)^* (00 + 11)^*$**
   - Any string generated by C consists of three sequential phases:
     - Phase 1: Zero or more repetitions of `10`
     - Phase 2: Zero or more repetitions of `01`
     - Phase 3: Zero or more repetitions of `00` or `11`
   - To match $w = 1101$:
     - $w$ cannot start with `10`, so Phase 1 must be $\varepsilon$.
     - $w$ cannot start with `01`, so Phase 2 must be $\varepsilon$.
     - This leaves the entire string $1101$ to be generated by $(00 + 11)^*$.
     - However, $(00 + 11)^*$ can only generate strings of even length consisting of pairs `00` and `11`. The string $1101$ has `01` as its last two characters, which cannot be generated.
   - Therefore, $1101$ **does not belong** to set C.

4. **Expression D: $(00 + (11)^* 0)^*$**
   - Look at the atomic building blocks of D:
     - Block 1: `00` (ends in `0`)
     - Block 2: $(11)^* 0$ (ends in `0`)
   - Every non-empty component in this expression **strictly ends with the character `0`**.
   - Consequently, every non-empty string generated by $(00 + (11)^* 0)^*$ must end in `0`.
   - Since $w = 1101$ ends in `1`, it is impossible to generate.
   - Therefore, $1101$ **does not belong** to set D.

### 3. Conclusion
The string $1101$ does not belong to sets **C** and **D**.

**Correct Answer: Options C and D**

go:1650.title: GATE CSE 1998 | Question: 1.13
go:1650.question:
What happens when a bit-string is XORed with itself $n$-times as shown:

$\left[B \oplus (B \oplus ( B \oplus (B \dots n \text{ times}\right]$

  1. complements when $n$ is even

  2. complements when $n$ is odd

  3. divides by $2^n$ always

  4. remains unchanged when $n$ is even

detailed_solution.concept: Digital Logic - Boolean XOR Properties and Parity Invariants
detailed_solution.markdown:
### 1. Problem Formulation & Governing Identities
We are given an expression where a bit-string $B$ is XORed with itself $n$ times:
$$E_n = \underbrace{B \oplus B \oplus B \oplus \dots \oplus B}_{n \text{ XOR operations on } n+1 \text{ operands}}$$
*Note on terminology:* "XORed with itself $n$ times" denotes applying $n$ XOR operations:
- $n = 1$: $B \oplus B$
- $n = 2$: $B \oplus B \oplus B$
- $n = 3$: $B \oplus B \oplus B \oplus B$

### 2. Fundamental Properties of XOR ($\oplus$)
1. **Nilpotence / Self-Inverse:**
   $$X \oplus X = 0$$
2. **Identity Element:**
   $$X \oplus 0 = X$$
3. **Associativity and Commutativity:**
   The grouping order does not affect the outcome.

### 3. Induction on the Number of XOR Operations $n$
- **For $n = 1$:**
  $$E_1 = B \oplus B = 0$$
- **For $n = 2$:**
  $$E_2 = (B \oplus B) \oplus B = 0 \oplus B = B \quad (\text{remains unchanged})$$
- **For $n = 3$:**
  $$E_3 = E_2 \oplus B = B \oplus B = 0$$
- **For $n = 4$:**
  $$E_4 = E_3 \oplus B = 0 \oplus B = B \quad (\text{remains unchanged})$$

In general, for any positive integer $k$:
- When $n = 2k$ (even number of operations):
  $$E_{2k} = B$$
  The bit-string **remains unchanged**.
- When $n = 2k - 1$ (odd number of operations):
  $$E_{2k-1} = 0$$

### 4. Distractor Analysis
- **Option A:** Fails; for even $n$, the result is $B$, not $\bar{B}$.
- **Option B:** Fails; for odd $n$, the result is $0$, not $\bar{B}$.
- **Option C:** Nonsensical arithmetic distractor.
- **Option D:** Correct; for any even $n$, an odd number of $B$'s are XORed together ($2k+1$ operands), leaving $B$ unchanged.

**Correct Answer: Option D**

go:1651.title: GATE CSE 1998 | Question: 1.14
go:1651.question:
A multiplexer with a $4-bit$ data select input is a

  1. $4:1$ multiplexer
  2. $2:1$ multiplexer
  3. $16:1$ multiplexer
  4. $8:1$ multiplexer

detailed_solution.concept: Digital Logic - Multiplexer Sizing and Select Line Relationships
detailed_solution.markdown:
### 1. Problem Formulation & Governing Formula
A multiplexer (data selector) routes one of $N$ input data lines to a single output line based on the binary combination applied to $k$ select inputs.

The governing relationship between the number of select lines $k$ and the number of data input lines $N$ is:
$$N = 2^k$$

### 2. Calculation for $k = 4$
Given:
- Number of select input bits: $k = 4$

Substituting into the formula:
$$N = 2^4 = 16 \text{ input data lines}$$

Therefore, a multiplexer with a $4$-bit data select input is a **$16$-to-$1$ ($16:1$) multiplexer**.

### 3. Distractor Analysis
- **Option A ($4:1$ multiplexer):** Requires $\log_2 4 = 2$ select bits.
- **Option B ($2:1$ multiplexer):** Requires $\log_2 2 = 1$ select bit.
- **Option C ($16:1$ multiplexer):** Correct; $2^4 = 16$ data inputs.
- **Option D ($8:1$ multiplexer):** Requires $\log_2 8 = 3$ select bits.

**Correct Answer: Option C**

go:1654.title: GATE CSE 1998 | Question: 1.17
go:1654.question:
The octal representation of an integer is $(342)_8$. If this were to be treated as an eight-bit integer in an $8085$ based computer, its decimal equivalent is

  1. $226$
  2. $-98$
  3. $76$
  4. $-30$

detailed_solution.concept: Digital Logic / Microprocessors - Octal to Two's Complement Decimal Conversion
detailed_solution.markdown:
### 1. Problem Formulation & Given Parameters
We are given an octal number:
$$N = (342)_8$$
We are asked for its decimal equivalent when treated as an **$8$-bit signed integer** in an $8085$-based computer.

### 2. Binary Conversion
Convert each octal digit to its $3$-bit binary equivalent:
- $3_8 = 011_2$
- $4_8 = 100_2$
- $2_8 = 010_2$

Concatenating gives the $9$-bit representation:
$$(342)_8 = 011100010_2$$

Because the $8085$ is an $8$-bit microprocessor, taking the low-order $8$ bits:
$$B = 11100010_2$$

### 3. Signed Decimal Evaluation ($2$'s Complement)
In $8085$ signed integer arithmetic, integers are represented in $8$-bit two's complement format:
- The Most Significant Bit (MSB, bit $7$) is $1$, indicating a **negative integer**.
- To determine the magnitude, compute the two's complement:
  1. Invert all bits:
     $$\sim (11100010_2) = 00011101_2$$
  2. Add $1$:
     $$00011101_2 + 1 = 00011110_2$$
  3. Convert binary magnitude to decimal:
     $$00011110_2 = 16 + 8 + 4 + 2 = 30_{10}$$

Attaching the negative sign:
$$\text{Decimal value} = -30$$

Alternatively, using positional weights:
$$\text{Value} = -1\cdot 2^7 + 1\cdot 2^6 + 1\cdot 2^5 + 0\cdot 2^4 + 0\cdot 2^3 + 0\cdot 2^2 + 1\cdot 2^1 + 0\cdot 2^0$$
$$= -128 + 64 + 32 + 2 = -128 + 98 = -30$$

**Correct Answer: Option D (-30)**

go:1655.title: GATE CSE 1998 | Question: 1.18
go:1655.question:
Which of the following devices should get higher priority in assigning interrupts?

  1. Hard disk
  2. Printer
  3. Keyboard
  4. Floppy disk

detailed_solution.concept: Operating Systems / Computer Architecture - Interrupt Priority Assignment
detailed_solution.markdown:
### 1. Conceptual Principle: Priority Assignment in Interrupt-Driven I/O
In computer architecture and operating system design, interrupt priority is assigned based on:
1. **Data Transfer Rate & Speed:** Faster peripheral devices transfer data at high rates and must be serviced quickly before internal FIFO buffers overflow.
2. **Criticality of Data Loss:** If a fast-moving physical medium (such as a spinning magnetic disk) is not serviced promptly, the read/write window passes, resulting in data loss, rotational latency penalties, or overrun errors.
3. **Latency Tolerance:** Slow human-interactive devices (such as keyboards) tolerate hundreds of milliseconds of delay without noticeable degradation.

### 2. Device Comparison
- **Hard Disk:** High-speed storage medium transferring megabytes per second. A sector read/write cannot pause; failure to service immediately results in data loss or disk transfer abortion. **Requires highest priority.**
- **Floppy Disk:** Moderate speed, transferring at tens of kilobytes per second (much slower than hard disk).
- **Printer:** Slow electromechanical output device operating at characters per second.
- **Keyboard:** Extremely low data rate (typically $\le 10\text{ bytes/s}$), highly latency tolerant.

### 3. Conclusion
The **hard disk** must receive the highest priority among the given devices.

**Correct Answer: Option A (Hard disk)**

go:1656.title: GATE CSE 1998 | Question: 1.19
go:1656.question:
Which of the following addressing modes permits relocation without any change whatsoever in the code?

  1. Indirect addressing

  2. Indexed addressing

  3. Base register addressing

  4. PC relative addressing

detailed_solution.concept: Computer Organization & Architecture - Position-Independent Code and PC-Relative Addressing
detailed_solution.markdown:
### 1. Conceptual Framework: Code Relocation
Code relocation is the ability to load and execute a compiled program module at any arbitrary base address in physical memory.
A program is **position-independent code (PIC)** if it can be loaded at different memory locations without requiring the loader to patch or recalculate any instruction addresses.

### 2. Analysis of Addressing Modes
- **PC-Relative Addressing:**
  - In PC-relative addressing, the effective target address is computed relative to the current value of the Program Counter ($PC$):
    $$\text{Effective Address} = PC + \text{Offset}$$
  - When the entire code block is relocated to a different memory region, both the instruction location ($PC$) and the target destination shift by the exact same distance.
  - Consequently, the displacement / offset remains completely invariant:
    $$\text{Offset} = \text{Target} - PC = \text{constant}$$
  - Thus, branch and jump instructions execute correctly without any modification whatsoever to the machine code.

- **Other Addressing Modes:**
  - **Indirect Addressing / Indexed Addressing:** Still require absolute base addresses or tables that must be initialized to physical addresses.
  - **Base Register Addressing:** Relocation requires updating the base register value at program start, whereas PC-relative addressing requires *zero change whatsoever* in either code or registers.

**Correct Answer: Option D (PC relative addressing)**

go:1657.title: GATE CSE 1998 | Question: 1.20
go:1657.question:
Which of the following is true?

  1. Unless enabled, a CPU will not be able to process interrupts.

  2. Loop instructions cannot be interrupted till they complete.

  3. A processor checks for interrupts before executing a new instruction.

  4. Only level triggered interrupts are possible on microprocessors.

detailed_solution.concept: Microprocessors / Operating Systems - Interrupt Handling and Processor Flags
detailed_solution.markdown:
### 1. Conceptual Framework & Evaluation of Statements
1. **Statement A: "Unless enabled, a CPU will not be able to process interrupts."**
   - **True.** General maskable hardware interrupts are gated by an internal interrupt-enable flip-flop (e.g., the Interrupt Flag `IF` in x86, or the `IE` flag in $8085$).
   - Upon system reset, maskable interrupts are disabled by default. Unless explicitly enabled via instructions such as `EI` (Enable Interrupts) in $8085$ or `STI` in x86, the CPU ignores all maskable interrupt requests.

2. **Statement B: "Loop instructions cannot be interrupted till they complete."**
   - **False.** Repeated or loop instructions (such as string primitives or loop counters) check for pending interrupts at each iteration cycle boundary and can be interrupted mid-loop.

3. **Statement C: "A processor checks for interrupts before executing a new instruction."**
   - **False.** A microprocessor samples and checks the interrupt lines at the **end of the execution phase** of the current instruction cycle (during the final T-state / machine cycle), not before.

4. **Statement D: "Only level triggered interrupts are possible on microprocessors."**
   - **False.** Microprocessors support both level-triggered (e.g., $8085$ `INTR`, `RST 5.5`) and edge-triggered interrupts (e.g., $8085$ `RST 7.5`, and `TRAP` which is edge-and-level sensitive).

### 2. Conclusion
The only true statement is **Option A**.

**Correct Answer: Option A**

go:1658.title: GATE CSE 1998 | Question: 1.21, ISRO2008-16
go:1658.question:
Which one of the following algorithm design techniques is used in finding all pairs of shortest distances in a graph?

  1. Dynamic programming

  2. Backtracking

  3. Greedy

  4. Divide and Conquer

detailed_solution.concept: Algorithms - All-Pairs Shortest Path and Dynamic Programming
detailed_solution.markdown:
### 1. Problem Formulation & Scope
We are asked to identify which algorithm design technique is utilized in finding all pairs of shortest distances in a directed or undirected graph.

### 2. Governing Algorithm: Floyd-Warshall Algorithm
The standard classical algorithm for solving the All-Pairs Shortest Path (APSP) problem in general weighted graphs (without negative weight cycles) is the **Floyd-Warshall algorithm**.

### 3. Mathematical Recurrence and Dynamic Programming Formulation
Let $V = \{1, 2, \dots, n\}$ be the vertex set of the graph.
Define $d_{ij}^{(k)}$ as the length of a shortest path from vertex $i$ to vertex $j$ such that all intermediate vertices on the path belong to the prefix set $\{1, 2, \dots, k\}$.

The algorithm computes these distances inductively using the following recurrence relation:
$$d_{ij}^{(k)} = \min\left(d_{ij}^{(k-1)}, \ d_{ik}^{(k-1)} + d_{kj}^{(k-1)}\right)$$
with the base cases:
$$d_{ij}^{(0)} = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } i = j \\ w(i, j) & \text{if } (i, j) \in E \\ \infty & \text{if } (i, j) \notin E \end{cases}$$

Because the problem exhibits:
1. **Optimal Substructure:** A shortest path between two vertices contains shortest subpaths between intermediate vertices.
2. **Overlapping Subproblems:** The computation of $d_{ij}^{(k)}$ reuses previously computed values $d_{ik}^{(k-1)}$ and $d_{kj}^{(k-1)}$ multiple times across different pairs $(i, j)$.

It is a quintessential application of the **Dynamic Programming** paradigm, operating with a time complexity of $\Theta(|V|^3)$ and space complexity of $\Theta(|V|^2)$.

### 4. Distractor Analysis
- **Option A (Dynamic programming):** Correct; Floyd-Warshall systematically builds shortest paths through intermediate vertices using dynamic programming.
- **Option B (Backtracking):** Used for constraint satisfaction problems (such as N-Queens, graph coloring, or Hamiltonian paths) where state space trees are pruned; not used for optimal all-pairs shortest path computation.
- **Option C (Greedy):** Used in single-source shortest path algorithms on graphs with non-negative edge weights (Dijkstra's algorithm, which makes locally optimal choices) and minimum spanning tree algorithms (Prim's and Kruskal's).
- **Option D (Divide and Conquer):** Solves independent, non-overlapping subproblems (such as in Merge Sort or Strassen's matrix multiplication).

### 5. Conclusion
Therefore, the correct algorithm design technique is **Dynamic programming**.

**Correct Answer: Option A**

go:1659.title: GATE CSE 1998 | Question: 1.22
go:1659.question:
Give the correct matching for the following pairs: $$\begin{array}{ll|ll}\hline \text{(A)} & \text{$O (\log n)$} & \text{(P)} & \text{Selection} \\\hline  \text{(B)} & \text{$O (n)$} & \text{(Q)}& \text{Insertion sort} \\\hline   \text{(C)}& \text{$O (n \log n)$} & \text{(R)}  & \text{Binary search} \\\hline  \text{(D)} & \text{$O (n^2)$} &\text{(S)}  & \text{Merge sort}  \\\hline \end{array}$$

  1. $\text{A-R  B-P  C-Q  D-S}$

  2. $\text{A-R  B-P  C-S  D-Q}$

  3. $\text{A-P  B-R  C-S  D-Q}$

  4. $\text{A-P  B-S  C-R  D-Q}$

detailed_solution.concept: Algorithms - Asymptotic Time Complexities of Classic Algorithms
detailed_solution.markdown:
### 1. Problem Formulation & Scope
We are required to match the given asymptotic time complexities with their corresponding algorithms:
- Time Complexities:
  - (A) $O(\log n)$
  - (B) $O(n)$
  - (C) $O(n \log n)$
  - (D) $O(n^2)$
- Algorithms:
  - (P) Selection
  - (Q) Insertion sort
  - (R) Binary search
  - (S) Merge sort

### 2. Analysis of Each Algorithm
1. **Binary Search (R):**
   - Operates on a sorted array of size $n$. At each comparison, the search interval is bisected in half.
   - Recurrence relation:
     $$T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1)$$
   - By Master Theorem: $T(n) = O(\log n)$.
   - Matches **(A)** $\implies$ **A-R**.

2. **Selection (P):**
   - The deterministic linear-time selection algorithm (Median-of-Medians / Quickselect worst-case, Blum-Floyd-Pratt-Rivest-Tarjan) finds the $k$-th smallest element in an unsorted array of size $n$.
   - Recurrence relation:
     $$T(n) \le T(n/5) + T(7n/10) + O(n)$$
   - Summing fractional subproblems: $\frac{1}{5} + \frac{7}{10} = \frac{9}{10} < 1$, yielding $T(n) = O(n)$.
   - Matches **(B)** $\implies$ **B-P**.

3. **Merge Sort (S):**
   - Divides the input array into two halves, recursively sorts each half, and merges the two sorted halves in linear time.
   - Recurrence relation:
     $$T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n)$$
   - In all cases (worst, average, and best), $T(n) = O(n \log n)$.
   - Matches **(C)** $\implies$ **C-S**.

4. **Insertion Sort (Q):**
   - Inserts each element into its sorted position within the prefix.
   - In the worst case (when the input array is reverse sorted), inserting the $i$-th element requires $i$ comparisons and shifts:
     $$\sum_{i=1}^{n-1} i = \frac{n(n-1)}{2} = O(n^2)$$
   - Matches **(D)** $\implies$ **D-Q**.

### 3. Conclusion & Matching
Combining the matches:
$$\text{A-R, \quad B-P, \quad C-S, \quad D-Q}$$

**Correct Answer: Option B**

go:1660.title: GATE CSE 1998 | Question: 1.23
go:1660.question:
How many sub strings of different lengths (non-zero) can be formed from a character string of length $n$?

  1. $n$
  2. $n^2$
  3. $2^n$
  4. $\frac{n(n+1)}{2}$

detailed_solution.concept: Discrete Mathematics - Combinatory
detailed_solution.markdown:
A substring is determined by its starting and ending positions. For length $1$ there are $n$ choices, for length $2$ there are $n-1$, and so on down to one substring of length $n$. Therefore,

$$n+(n-1)+\cdots+1=\frac{n(n+1)}2.$$

**Option D.**

go:1661.title: GATE CSE 1998 | Question: 1.24
go:1661.question:
Which of the following statements is false?

  1.  A tree with a $n$ nodes has $(n – 1)$ edges
  2.  A labeled rooted binary tree can be uniquely constructed given its postorder and preorder traversal results.
  3.  A complete binary tree with $n$ internal nodes has $(n + 1)$ leaves.
  4.  The maximum number of nodes in a binary tree of height h is $2^{h+1} - 1$

detailed_solution.concept: Programming and DS - Properties and Traversal Invariants of Binary Trees
detailed_solution.markdown:
### 1. Problem Formulation & Scope
We are required to identify which of the four statements regarding trees and binary trees is **false**.

### 2. Analytical Evaluation of Statements
1. **Statement A: "A tree with $n$ nodes has $(n - 1)$ edges"**
   - By definition, a tree is a connected acyclic undirected graph.
   - A fundamental theorem of graph theory states that any connected graph with $n$ vertices and no cycles possesses exactly $n - 1$ edges.
   - Therefore, Statement A is **TRUE**.

2. **Statement B: "A labeled rooted binary tree can be uniquely constructed given its postorder and preorder traversal results."**
   - Preorder traversal visits: $\text{Root} \to \text{Left} \to \text{Right}$.
   - Postorder traversal visits: $\text{Left} \to \text{Right} \to \text{Root}$.
   - While preorder and postorder traversals allow us to identify the root and its subtrees in a *strict/full* binary tree (where every internal node has exactly $2$ children), they **cannot** distinguish between a single left child and a single right child for a node with degree $1$.
   - *Counterexample:* Consider a tree with two nodes, $A$ and $B$:
     - Tree 1: Root $A$, with $B$ as its left child.
       - Preorder: $A, B$
       - Postorder: $B, A$
     - Tree 2: Root $A$, with $B$ as its right child.
       - Preorder: $A, B$
       - Postorder: $B, A$
     Both distinct trees produce identical preorder and postorder sequences. Without an inorder traversal, the tree cannot be uniquely constructed.
   - Therefore, Statement B is **FALSE**.

3. **Statement C: "A complete binary tree with $n$ internal nodes has $(n + 1)$ leaves."**
   - In standard classical textbook terminology (Horowitz & Sahni, Cormen), a complete/strict binary tree where every internal node has degree $2$ satisfies the leaf-internal relation:
     $$L = I + 1 = n + 1$$
   - Therefore, Statement C is **TRUE**.

4. **Statement D: "The maximum number of nodes in a binary tree of height $h$ is $2^{h+1} - 1$"**
   - With the root at level $0$ (height $0$), the maximum number of nodes at level $i$ is $2^i$.
   - Summing across levels $0$ to $h$:
     $$\sum_{i=0}^h 2^i = 2^{h+1} - 1$$
   - Therefore, Statement D is **TRUE**.

### 3. Conclusion
The statement that is false is Statement B.

**Correct Answer: Option B**

go:1662.title: GATE CSE 1998 | Question: 1.25, ISRO2008-41
go:1662.question:
In a resident – OS computer, which of the following systems must reside in the main memory under all situations?

  1. Assembler
  2. Linker
  3. Loader
  4. Compiler

detailed_solution.concept: Compiler Design / Operating Systems - System Software & Resident Memory Requirements
detailed_solution.markdown:
### 1. Conceptual Framework: System Software Lifecycle
In a resident operating system environment, different system software tools operate during distinct phases of the program lifecycle:
- **Translation / Compilation:** Translates human-readable high-level source code into assembly or relocatable machine code.
- **Assembly:** Converts assembly language mnemonics into relocatable object code modules.
- **Linking:** Combines independently compiled relocatable object modules and library routines, resolving external symbol references.
- **Loading & Execution:** Transfers the executable machine binary from secondary storage into physical main memory (RAM) and passes execution control to the program entry point.

### 2. Resident vs. Transient System Programs
1. **Compilers, Assemblers, and Linkers:**
   - These are development tools. They are invoked only on demand when a program is being written or built.
   - They reside on secondary storage (disk) as regular executable files and are loaded into RAM only during translation, after which their memory is reclaimed.
   - A running computer executing existing applications has zero need for a compiler, assembler, or linker to be present in main memory.

2. **The Loader:**
   - The loader (or the resident program execution loader module of the OS kernel) is responsible for taking an executable binary from disk, assigning physical addresses (relocation), setting up the initial program stack and heap, and launching the process.
   - In order for the operating system to launch and run *any* application or command, the loader must be immediately available. Hence, the loader (as part of the resident OS kernel) must reside in main memory under all operating conditions.

### 3. Conclusion
Therefore, the **Loader** must reside in main memory under all situations.

**Correct Answer: Option C (Loader)**

go:1663.title: GATE CSE 1998 | Question: 1.26
go:1663.question:
Which of the following statements is true?

  1. SLR parser is more powerful than LALR

  2. LALR parser is more powerful than Canonical LR parser

  3. Canonical LR parser is more powerful than LALR parser

  4. The parsers SLR, Canonical CR, and LALR have the same power

detailed_solution.concept: Compiler Design - Relative Expressive Power of LR Parsers
detailed_solution.markdown:
### 1. Conceptual Framework & Parser Hierarchy
In bottom-up (shift-reduce) parsing for Context-Free Grammars (CFGs), parsers utilizing a single lookahead token are classified by their parsing power:
$$\text{LR}(0) \subsetneq \text{SLR}(1) \subsetneq \text{LALR}(1) \subsetneq \text{CLR}(1) \text{ (Canonical LR(1))}$$

A parser class $\mathcal{P}_1$ is defined as more powerful than class $\mathcal{P}_2$ if the family of grammars parsable without conflict by $\mathcal{P}_1$ strictly subsumes the family of grammars parsable by $\mathcal{P}_2$.

### 2. Analytical Comparison of SLR, LALR, and CLR
1. **SLR(1) vs. LALR(1):**
   - SLR(1) uses $\text{LR}(0)$ item states and uses the global $\text{FOLLOW}(A)$ set to decide reduce actions. This coarse global follow set frequently causes spurious reduce/reduce and shift/reduce conflicts.
   - LALR(1) uses context-specific lookahead symbols generated during item construction, making $\text{LALR}(1)$ strictly more powerful than $\text{SLR}(1)$.

2. **LALR(1) vs. CLR(1):**
   - CLR(1) (Canonical LR) constructs the complete collection of $\text{LR}(1)$ states without any state merging, retaining the full context for each lookahead symbol.
   - LALR(1) merges states of CLR(1) that have identical $\text{LR}(0)$ cores.
   - While state merging in LALR(1) never introduces new shift/reduce conflicts, it **can introduce reduce/reduce conflicts**.
   - Consequently, there exist valid context-free grammars that can be parsed deterministically by CLR(1) but cannot be parsed by LALR(1).
   - Thus, **Canonical LR parser is strictly more powerful than LALR parser**.

### 3. Distractor Analysis
- **Option A:** False; SLR is strictly less powerful than LALR.
- **Option B:** False; LALR is strictly less powerful than CLR.
- **Option C:** True; Canonical LR parser has the greatest language coverage and power without merging states.
- **Option D:** False; they have strictly different parsing capabilities.

### 4. Conclusion
Therefore, the true statement is **Canonical LR parser is more powerful than LALR parser**.

**Correct Answer: Option C**

go:1664.title: GATE CSE 1998 | Question: 1.27
go:1664.question:
Type checking is normally done during

  1. lexical analysis
  2. syntax analysis
  3. syntax directed translation
  4. code optimization

detailed_solution.concept: Compiler Design - Semantic Analysis and Type Checking Phase
detailed_solution.markdown:
### 1. Conceptual Framework: Phases of a Compiler
A standard language compiler operates across six classic sequential phases:
1. **Lexical Analysis (Scanner):** Converts stream of characters into lexical tokens; strips whitespace and comments.
2. **Syntax Analysis (Parser):** Validates tokens against grammar productions and builds a parse tree or abstract syntax tree (AST).
3. **Semantic Analysis / Syntax Directed Translation (SDT):**
   - Checks semantic consistency with the language definition.
   - Evaluates type expressions, performs **type checking**, checks compatibility in assignments and operators, handles implicit type coercions, and validates variable declaration scopes.
   - This phase is typically implemented using **Syntax-Directed Translation schemes (SDTS)** and attributed parse trees.
4. **Intermediate Code Generation:** Generates machine-independent intermediate representations (such as three-address code).
5. **Code Optimization:** Improves code performance and reduces resource consumption without altering program semantics.
6. **Code Generation:** Emits target assembly or machine code.

### 2. Distractor Analysis
- **Option A (lexical analysis):** Only checks token spelling and character validity; has no concept of types, variables, or expressions.
- **Option B (syntax analysis):** Only checks grammatical structure; cannot determine whether an identifier is an integer, pointer, or float.
- **Option C (syntax directed translation):** Correct; type synthesis, checking, and attribute decoration are performed during semantic analysis via syntax-directed translation.
- **Option D (code optimization):** Operates on intermediate code after all types have already been checked and validated.

### 3. Conclusion
Therefore, type checking is normally done during **syntax directed translation**.

**Correct Answer: Option C**

go:1665.title: GATE CSE 1998 | Question: 1.28
go:1665.question:
A linker reads four modules whose lengths are $200, 800, 600$ and $500$ words, respectively. If they are loaded in that order, what are the relocation constants?

  1. $0, 200, 500, 600$
  2. $0, 200, 1000, 1600$
  3. $200, 500, 600, 800$
  4. $200, 700, 1300, 2100$

detailed_solution.concept: System Software / Linkers & Loaders - Relocation Constants Calculation
detailed_solution.markdown:
### 1. Problem Formulation & Given Parameters
A linker reads four program modules with the following lengths:
- Length of Module 1: $L_1 = 200$ words
- Length of Module 2: $L_2 = 800$ words
- Length of Module 3: $L_3 = 600$ words
- Length of Module 4: $L_4 = 500$ words

The modules are concatenated and loaded sequentially into contiguous memory starting at address $0$. We are required to determine the **relocation constants** for each of the four modules.

### 2. Governing Principle: Relocation Constant
In linking and loading, the **relocation constant** (or relocation factor / load base) of a module is the offset address added to every relative address within that module to map it to its physical load location:
$$\text{Relocation Constant}_k = \text{Starting Address of Module } k$$

### 3. Step-by-Step Calculation
- **Module 1:**
  - Placed at base address: $0$
  - Relocation constant: $R_1 = 0$
  - Occupies address range: $[0, \ 0 + 200 - 1] = [0, \ 199]$

- **Module 2:**
  - Placed immediately after Module 1:
    $$R_2 = R_1 + L_1 = 0 + 200 = 200$$
  - Occupies address range: $[200, \ 200 + 800 - 1] = [200, \ 999]$

- **Module 3:**
  - Placed immediately after Module 2:
    $$R_3 = R_2 + L_2 = 200 + 800 = 1000$$
  - Occupies address range: $[1000, \ 1000 + 600 - 1] = [1000, \ 1599]$

- **Module 4:**
  - Placed immediately after Module 3:
    $$R_4 = R_3 + L_3 = 1000 + 600 = 1600$$
  - Occupies address range: $[1600, \ 1600 + 500 - 1] = [1600, \ 2099]$

### 4. Sequence of Relocation Constants
The relocation constants in the order of loading are:
$$0, \quad 200, \quad 1000, \quad 1600$$

**Correct Answer: Option B**

go:1666.title: GATE CSE 1998 | Question: 1.29
go:1666.question:
Which of the following is an example of a spooled device?

  1. The terminal used to enter the input data for the C program being executed

  2. An output device used to print the output of a number of jobs

  3. The secondary memory device in a virtual storage system

  4. The swapping area on a disk used by the swapper

detailed_solution.concept: Operating Systems - Spooling and Shared Peripheral Management
detailed_solution.markdown:
### 1. Conceptual Framework: Spooling
**SPOOL** is an acronym for **Simultaneous Peripheral Operations On-Line**.
Spooling is a technique that uses secondary storage (a disk buffer) as a large staging area to manage data transfers between processes and slow, dedicated, non-sharable I/O peripherals.

### 2. Characteristics of Spooled Devices
- Certain peripheral devices, notably **line printers** or plotters, cannot accept interleaved characters from multiple concurrent processes. If two processes attempted to write directly to a shared printer simultaneously, lines of text from both jobs would be chaotically interleaved on the paper.
- To prevent this, the operating system intercepts print outputs and writes them into separate temporary files on disk (the spool directory).
- Once an entire print job is completely generated and closed, the spooler daemon transfers the file sequentially to the physical printer.
- Thus, an output printer serving multiple concurrent jobs is the classic textbook embodiment of a **spooled device**.

### 3. Distractor Analysis
- **Option A (terminal used to enter input data):** An interactive character-by-character input device; not a spooled device.
- **Option B (output device used to print the output of a number of jobs):** Correct; standard definition and primary application of spooling.
- **Option C (secondary memory device in a virtual storage system):** Paging and swap disks are backing stores for virtual memory, not spooled devices.
- **Option D (swapping area on a disk used by the swapper):** Part of memory management infrastructure, not a spooled peripheral.

### 4. Conclusion
Therefore, an output device used to print the output of a number of jobs is an example of a spooled device.

**Correct Answer: Option B**

go:1667.title: GATE CSE 1998 | Question: 1.30
go:1667.question:
When the result of a computation depends on the speed of the processes involved, there is said to be

  1. cycle stealing
  2. race condition
  3. a time lock
  4. a deadlock

detailed_solution.concept: Operating Systems - Process Synchronization and Race Conditions
detailed_solution.markdown:
### 1. Problem Formulation & Scope
We are asked to identify the concurrency phenomenon where the final outcome of a computation depends on the execution speeds or scheduling order of the participating processes.

### 2. Definition & Mechanism: Race Condition
A **race condition** occurs in concurrent and multi-threaded systems when:
1. Two or more concurrent processes access and manipulate shared data or resources concurrently.
2. At least one of the processes performs a write (modification) operation.
3. The final result of the computation depends directly on the relative execution speeds, interleaving, or specific order in which instructions are executed.

To prevent race conditions, critical sections must be protected using mutual exclusion mechanisms (such as semaphores, mutex locks, or monitors).

### 3. Distractor Analysis
- **Option A (cycle stealing):** A direct memory access (DMA) technique where the DMA controller temporarily takes control of the system bus for one bus cycle to transfer a byte/word, pausing the CPU momentarily.
- **Option B (race condition):** Correct; the canonical definition of a race condition.
- **Option C (a time lock):** A non-standard, fictitious term in operating system theory.
- **Option D (a deadlock):** A state where a set of processes are permanently blocked because each process holds resources and waits for resources held by others in the set.

### 4. Conclusion
Therefore, the condition where the result depends on process speeds is called a **race condition**.

**Correct Answer: Option B**

go:1668.title: GATE CSE 1998 | Question: 1.31
go:1668.question:
A counting semaphore was initialized to $10$. Then $6 P$ (wait) operations and $4V$ (signal) operations were completed on this semaphore. The resulting value of the semaphore is

  1. $0$
  2. $8$
  3. $10$
  4. $12$

detailed_solution.concept: Operating Systems - Counting Semaphore State Transitions
detailed_solution.markdown:
### 1. Conceptual Framework & Governing Definitions
A counting semaphore $S$ is an integer variable accessed exclusively through two standard atomic primitives:
1. **$P$ operation (Wait / Down):**
   Decrements the semaphore value:
   $$S \leftarrow S - 1$$
   (If $S < 0$, the calling process is blocked).
2. **$V$ operation (Signal / Up):**
   Increments the semaphore value:
   $$S \leftarrow S + 1$$
   (If $S \le 0$, a blocked process is awakened).

### 2. Step-by-Step State Evolution
- **Initial Value:**
  $$S_0 = 10$$
- **Execution of $6 \ P$ Operations:**
  Each $P$ operation decrements the semaphore counter by $1$:
  $$S_1 = S_0 - 6 = 10 - 6 = 4$$
- **Execution of $4 \ V$ Operations:**
  Each $V$ operation increments the semaphore counter by $1$:
  $$S_2 = S_1 + 4 = 4 + 4 = 8$$

### 3. Conclusion
The resulting value of the semaphore after all operations are completed is **8**.

**Correct Answer: Option B**

go:1669.title: GATE CSE 1998 | Question: 1.32
go:1669.question:
A computer has six tape drives, with $n$ processes competing for them. Each process may need two drives. What is the maximum value of $n$ for the system to be deadlock free?

  1. $6$
  2. $5$
  3. $4$
  4. $3$

detailed_solution.concept: Operating Systems - Deadlock Prevention and Resource Allocation Bounds
detailed_solution.markdown:
### 1. Problem Formulation & Given Parameters
We are given:
- Total number of identical tape drives: $m = 6$
- Number of competing processes: $n$
- Maximum resource requirement of each process: $M = 2$ drives

We need to determine the maximum value of $n$ such that the system is guaranteed to be **deadlock-free**.

### 2. Governing Principle: Deadlock Prevention Threshold
By the Pigeonhole Principle applied to resource allocation, a deadlock occurs if and only if every process has acquired one unit less than its maximum requirement and is waiting for its final resource, but no free resources remain:
$$\text{Worst-case allocated resources} = \sum_{i=1}^n (M - 1) = n(2 - 1) = n$$

For the system to be **guaranteed deadlock-free** under all possible allocation sequences, the total number of resources $m$ must strictly exceed this worst-case allocation by at least $1$, ensuring at least one process can satisfy its full requirement, complete execution, and return all its resources to the available pool:
$$m \ge n(M - 1) + 1$$

### 3. Analytical Derivation
Substitute the given values ($m = 6, M = 2$):
$$6 \ge n(2 - 1) + 1$$
$$6 \ge n + 1$$
$$n \le 5$$

- **For $n = 5$:** In the worst-case state, each of the 5 processes holds 1 tape drive (total 5 drives allocated). Since $m = 6$, there is $6 - 5 = 1$ tape drive remaining free. This drive can be allocated to any process, allowing it to satisfy its maximum demand of 2, finish execution, and release both drives. Hence, deadlock is impossible.
- **For $n = 6$:** Each of the 6 processes could hold 1 drive (total 6 drives allocated). With 0 drives remaining free, every process is waiting for a drive held by another process, causing a circular wait and a deadlock.

Thus, the maximum value of $n$ for the system to remain deadlock-free is **5**.

**Correct Answer: Option B**

go:1671.title: GATE CSE 1998 | Question: 1.34
go:1671.question:
Which normal form is considered adequate for normal relational database design?

  1. $2NF$
  2. $5NF$
  3. $4NF$
  4. $3NF$

detailed_solution.concept: Databases - Normal Forms in Relational Database Design (3NF)
detailed_solution.markdown:
### 1. Conceptual Framework: Normalization Goals
Relational database normalization organizes tables and attributes to minimize data redundancy and avoid insertion, deletion, and update anomalies while preserving data integrity.

### 2. Criteria for an Adequate Relational Schema Design
A satisfactory relational database design must fulfill two fundamental mathematical properties:
1. **Lossless-Join Decomposition:** Guaranteeing that natural joins reconstruct the original relations without generating spurious tuples.
2. **Dependency Preservation:** Ensuring that all functional dependencies in the original schema can be verified within individual relations without computing expensive relational joins.

### 3. Normal Form Comparison
- **1NF:** Eliminates composite and multivalued attributes (ensures atomic domains), but permits severe partial and transitive redundancy.
- **2NF:** Eliminates partial functional dependencies of non-prime attributes on candidate keys, but permits transitive dependencies.
- **3NF (Third Normal Form):**
  - Eliminates all transitive dependencies of non-prime attributes on candidate keys.
  - Formally, for every non-trivial functional dependency $X \to Y$, either $X$ is a superkey or $Y$ is a prime attribute.
  - **Crucially, it is always mathematically possible to achieve a 3NF decomposition that is simultaneously Lossless-Join AND Dependency-Preserving.**
- **BCNF, 4NF, 5NF:** While BCNF eliminates all redundancy from functional dependencies, a dependency-preserving BCNF decomposition is not always achievable.
- Consequently, standard database theory (Elmasri & Navathe, Silberschatz) establishes **3NF** as the benchmark normal form that is "considered adequate for normal relational database design".

**Correct Answer: Option D (3NF)**

go:1672.title: GATE CSE 1998 | Question: 1.35
go:1672.question:
There are five records in a database.
$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|} \hline \textbf {Name} & \textbf {Age} & \textbf {Occupation} &  \textbf{Category } \\\hline \text{Rama} & \text{27} & \text{CON} & \text{A} \\\hline \text{Abdul} & \text{22} & \text{ENG} & \text{A} \\\hline \text{Jennifer} & \text{28} & \text{DOC} & \text{B} \\\hline \text{Maya} & \text{32} & \text{SER} & \text{D} \\\hline \text{Dev} & \text{24} & \text{MUS} & \text{C} \\\hline \end{array}$$

There is an index file associated with this and it contains the values $1, 3, 2, 5$ and $4$. Which one of the fields is the index built from?

  1. Age
  2. Name
  3. Occupation
  4. Category

detailed_solution.concept: Databases - Search Key Identification from Index Order
detailed_solution.markdown:
### 1. Problem Formulation & Given Database Records
We are given five database records with 1-based record identification numbers:
$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|}
\hline
\textbf{Record \#} & \textbf{Name} & \textbf{Age} & \textbf{Occupation} & \textbf{Category} \\
\hline
1 & \text{Rama} & 27 & \text{CON} & \text{A} \\
2 & \text{Abdul} & 22 & \text{ENG} & \text{A} \\

An index file associates the physical record numbers in the following sequence:
$$\text{Index Sequence: } 1, \ 3, \ 2, \ 5, \ 4$$

We must determine which attribute was used as the search key to build the index.

### 2. Governing Principle: Ordered Index Files
An index file stores search-key values along with record pointers sorted in **ascending order** of the indexed search key. Therefore, the values of the indexed field corresponding to the sequence $1, 3, 2, 5, 4$ must be strictly sorted.

### 3. Testing Each Candidate Field
1. **Occupation:**
   - Record 1: $\text{CON}$
   - Record 3: $\text{DOC}$
   - Record 2: $\text{ENG}$
   - Record 5: $\text{MUS}$

   Checking alphabetical order:
   $$\text{CON} < \text{DOC} < \text{ENG} < \text{MUS} < \text{SER}$$
   The sequence of initial characters is:
   $$\text{'C'} \ (\text{CON}) < \text{'D'} \ (\text{DOC}) < \text{'E'} \ (\text{ENG}) < \text{'M'} \ (\text{MUS}) < \text{'S'} \ (\text{SER})$$
   This sequence is in **perfect ascending alphabetical order**!

2. **Age:**

3. **Name:**
   - Record order values: $\text{Rama}, \text{Jennifer}, \text{Abdul}, \text{Dev}, \text{Maya}$

4. **Category:**
